newsitem.title: USA: Fed unveils new computer model to forecast economy.
newsitem.headline: Fed unveils new computer model to forecast economy.

text.p: The Federal Reserve has created a new computer forecasting model that elevates the role that expectations of consumers, businesses and investors play in the economy, central bank economists said on Friday.
The new model for analyzing the domestic economy, called the "FRB/US," replaces one that the Fed has been using since the 1960s and is the culmination of several years of research.
Containing about 300 equations, the model is being used for short-run forecasting and for analysis of monetary policy, according to a paper presented here by four Fed economists.
The Fed also has a world economic model that links the new domestic equations to foreign country models.

The idea of emphasizing the expectations of financial market players, businesses and consumers stems from research during the 1970s by Nobel laureate Robert Lucas on the role of "rational expectations" that has achieved a great deal of prominence in the economics profession.

The paper by Fed economists Flint Brayton, Andrew Levin, Ralph Tyron and John Williams, to the Carnegie-Rochester monetary policy conference here, highlights a number of policy uses for the new model.
In one example, the domestic model was used to examine the impact of the central bank's credibility on the process of reducing inflation.
The finding was that a high degree of confidence in a central bank can allow it to push inflation lower with less cost to economic output.

Such a situation arises when bond markets become accustomed to "anticipating" potential monetary tightenings, leading to a rise in long-term rates that allows the central bank to fight inflation without clamping down as forcefully on credit.
"Under imperfect credibility of monetary policy, the extra leverage from a full and immediate reduction in inflation expectations is absent," the paper pointed out.

"Thus, the monetary authority must dampen aggregate demand and lower observed inflation through higher real interest rates in order to convince the private sector of its determination to disinflate," it said.

In a separate paper to the conference, other Fed economists said central bank staffers use an array of sophisticated models to help chart the course of the economy, but ultimately their forecasts blend both art and science.

David Reifschneider, David Stockton and David Wilcox said that computer models alone are insufficient for the analysis that is needed to set interest-rate policy and that human judgement must also play a role.according to a paper presented here by four Fed economists.
